articles.text: Cost estimates soar to $6 million over budget The Piedmont Community Pool project is $6 million over budget according to a hard cost estimate, necessitating that the conceptual design be trimmed. Piedmont City Council discussed the matter at a March 21 meeting, and approved the modifications proposed by city staff and ELS Architecture and Urban Design, the firm chosen to lead the design process. The city council approved a design on January 18 after considering feedback received in three community workshops and reports from five publicly-held Pool Advisory Committee meetings held between October 2021 and February 2022. ELS completed the schematic design process on March 4 and sent a schematic design package to City Council, including construction cost estimates. The Emeryville-based construction management and consulting firm Mack5 analyzed ELS’ design elements and provided the City with a cost estimate; it far exceeded the city’s target budget. “Mack5’s analysis of the design elements resulted in a ‘hard cost’ construction cost estimate of roughly $25 million which far exceeds the city’s target of $19 million. We are faced with a $6 million gap as we move toward design development,” Lillevand said, adding that the extraordinary cost estimates will necessitate a reduction of the original design. “These modifications, while significant and disappointing, do continue to meet the aquatic needs of the community,” Lillevand said. The primary reason for higher-than-anticipated costs is hyperinflation, Lillevand explained. Construction industry experts also advise that construction costs will rise at a rate in excess of 1% per month. Modifications to design Clarence Mamuyac, President of ELS, provided a design update to city council on March 21. articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: Whichever decision you make with regard to how the pools will be heated, you can expect issues to come up during construction, with a subset of problems having to be brought to your attention. Sleep loss is inherent to the fate of people who build real stuff! If you select an all-electric solution, it is likely that the number of headaches will be higher, given that Piedmont will be innovating in deploying a proven technology for a new use (for sure in California). But our community will have the satisfaction of showing other municipalities the way to create aquatics facilities as green as possible: an important case study for our State. I am confident that given the quality of the City staff, the contractor and consultants involved that you will make an informed decision weighing technical considerations, capital and operational expenses, environmental issues, the uncertainty of the relative future costs of different energy sources and inflation. As Piedmonters, we elect you to make the tough decisions, and regardless of the way you choose, taking a prudent approach, a trailblazer one, or something in-between, I encourage our community to support your decision. I certainly will. –Bernard Pech For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont tonight, Wednesday, March 30, for a discussion with Dr. Fiona Hill, Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution at Stanford. The Zoom episode will explore the current state of democracy, from both domestic and international points of view. Dr. Hill is the Robert Bosch Senior Fellow at the Center on the United States and Europe in the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution and member of the Council on Foreign Relations. Her most recent book, There is Nothing for You Here, draws on her personal journey out of poverty, as well as her unique perspectives as a historian and policy maker, to show how we can return hope to our forgotten places. From 2017 to 2019, Dr. Hill served as deputy assistant to the president and senior director for European and Russian affairs on the National Security Council. From 2006 to 2009, she served as national intelligence officer for Russia and Eurasia at the National Intelligence Council. She has researched and published extensively on issues related to Russia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, regional conflicts, energy, and strategic issues. Co-author of Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin and The Siberian Curse: How Communist Planners Left Russia Out in the Cold, she holds a master’s degree in Soviet studies and a doctorate in history from Harvard University and a master’s in Russian and modern history from St. Andrews University in Scotland. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in California, Oregon, Colorado, and Florida. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website Dr. Fiona Hill is the guest speaker of a League of Women Voters discussion on Russia tonight, March 30. lwvpiedmont.org to learn more about the series and register for this event. Once you have registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual discussion on equitable real estate practices that support an inclusive community on April 7 via Zoom. The event, entitled “Welcome to Piedmont: Real Estate Practices in Support of an Inclusive Community,” is co-sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV), Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC). The discussion will be moderated by Carol Galante, a Piedmont resident and founder of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley. The panelists include retired Piedmont real estate agent Maureen Kennedy, a former member of the Clinton Administration; Chief Diversity and Equity Officer at California Association of Realtors Farrah Wilder; and Ashley Gardner, Community Outreach Coordinator for California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). Residents and real estate professionals who tune in will learn about what the current context for real estate practices and its impact on the demographics of the Piedmont community. A moderated discussion between the above professionals will focus on the benefits of an inclusive community and how Piedmont residents can help affirm the city’s commitment to be a more welcoming and diverse community. “Real estate transactions and the interplay between sellers, real estate professionals and potential buyers is one piece of a complex puzzle we are striving to solve... how to bring more diversity to Piedmont,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “We look forward to an engaging dialogue focused on evolving practices and new ideas to help shape the Piedmont of the future.” In September 2021, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law over 30 affordable housing bills that focused on cutting red tape and holding cities accountable for providing their fair share of housing. When signing the legislation, he said “[the] bills, plus [last] year’s historic budget investments in affordable housing, will directly lead to more inclusive neighborhoods across the state. Creating denser housing near jobs, parks and schools is key to meeting our climate goals as well as our affordability goals.” To participate in this event, use the Zoom Registration Link at https://piedmont-ca-gov. zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_ zGnJ-AWnT4KFzrNxe2mKlg.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will perform William Golding’s Lord of the Flies in five performances from Thursday through Sunday, March 31 to April 3. The novel Lord of the Flies, adapted for the stage by Nigel Williams, is part of Piedmont’s freshman year English curriculum. Williams’ stage adaptation follows the plot of the novel – a group of British boys get stranded and are forced to face horrifying beasties on an island after their plane crashes on the island. Acting students of all genders will perform roles as the English boys, including speaking with a British dialect. What happens when young boys are left alone on an island with no structure? “The answer is pretty terrifying,” said cast member PHS junior Chloe Kibarian. The production is rated PG-13 for violence. The cast features Advanced Acting juniors and seniors Theo Arenstam (Simon-Sat, Sun 6pm), Liam Gordon (Simon-Thurs, Fri, Sun 1pm), Milani Juarbe (Robert), Sarone Kelete (Henry), Chloe Kibarian (Perceval-Fri/ Sun), Molly McWeeny (Piggy), Fernanda Meagher (Roger), Izzy Rosselli (Maurice), Erik Stenstrom (Eric), Joyce Stern (Ralph), Katherine Stormer (Perceval-Thurs/Sat), Holden Temple (Jack), John Gross Whitaker (Sam), and Charles E. White (Henry). Director Kimberly Taylor said, “I am grateful that the class is able to perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts once more after the last successful collaboration there for the production of Lisa Loomer’s Roe immediately prior to the pandemic shutdown in March 2020. The Piedmont Center for the Arts allows us the flexibility to create unique seating configurations. For this show, audience members will be close to the action and will feel like they’re on the island, too,” she said. Lord of the Flies performances are Thursday through Saturday, March 31 to April 2 at 7:00 p.m., with two performances on Sunday, April 3 at 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. Tickets are $10 for students and $17 for general admission. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue across the street from the high school. All events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts require audience members to present proof of full vaccination plus booster, as well as proper masking inside. articles.text: On Friday, March 24, this reporter received an invitation to Ted Scherman’s 7th grade core class for an Inside the Classroom story. Instead of sitting in the back of the class to take notes for a story on the students studies, I was asked to stand at the front and take the microphone. The students were studying about the Protestant Reformation, and they had decided to create a newspaper. So I donned my press pass, and arrived with a recorder, camera, and typewriter to encourage all the budding journalists. I placed my Royal Safari typewriter, a DSLR camera, and copies of the Post on a desk for everyone to see, touch, and use. The students were attentive, polite and seemed genuinely interested in writing and journalism. I did my best to impart to them how much I enjoy getting to meet new people doing extraordinary things every week, and added a few secrets of the trade. We talked about the importance of receiving consent for recording audio, the California laws on paparazzi, and fair use for taking photos in public. I pointed out the press box in the paper, the proficiency of the Post’s city editor Allyson Aleksey, and we discussed why a writer might want to use a pseudonym (pen name). Scherman asked about the state of print journalism versus digital. I suggested that online publications are still in a wild west-like stage, and looking for ways to charge for content. During COVID, despite news being consumed at a high level, the number of newspapers that went out of business increased by the hundreds. However, I shared my observation and belief that there is a nostalgia for printed newspapers. Now it was time for the students to be part of the story I would be writing, so I turned the camera over to a couple of Piedmont Post delivery kids in the class, Henry Call and Colby Hong, hoping they were as good at photography as they were at chucking a paper to front doors. After describing the camera’s features, they took a few photos to get photo credits for this article. After handing out copies of the Post I asked for observations and received some of the following questions: What is the difference between a feature and a news story? How did the author get these photos? Do you ever get writer’s block? What do you do to get rid of it? The last question gave me the opportunity to introduce my typewriter, a somewhat ancient relic, a Royal Safari, circa 1965. There is something rewarding about seeing your words instantly in print, hearing the clickity clack of the typebar’s anvils hitting the paper, and the ding of the bell at the end of each line being typed onto a page. Another strategy to tackle writer’s block relies on far more contemporary technology, using Photos by Henry Call, Colby Hong, and Ted Scherman Daniela Lucaccin (left), Elsa Wallway, Claire Aubrecht, Thomas Moision and Colby Hong try their hand at writing poetry. the voice-to-text feature on a phone. (I am of generation Y, after all.) Students found that strategy more palatable than anything involving the 40-pound keyboard in front of them, a machine older than most of their parents. After the talk, students came to the front to try it out and learn how a typewriter ribbon works. After a few failed attempts by students, I explained the keys had to be pressed down much harder than on a computer and introduced the “hunt-and peck” two-finger typing style to some of them. When it looked like the typebars were jammed and the machine broken, the students learned about the “margin release” key. They were impressed that the typewriter ribbon had two colors, red and black. If they weren’t so well-mannered, they might have called me crazy when I explained that I had to re-ink the ribbon with a paint brush and stamp pad ink, one inch at a time. After gathering my stuff and saying goodbye, the students turned their attention to their daily lesson, watching a current events show and then creating their own fake Instagram or Facebook pages of someone from the Renaissance era. With the class back in the hands of the veteran teacher, I returned to my comfortable post at the Post, with a renewed appreciation for teachers and the remarkable curiosity of Mr. Scherman’s students. I did my best to impart to them how much I enjoy getting to meet new people doing extraordinary things every week, and added a few secrets of the trade. We talked about the importance of receiving consent for recording audio, the California laws on paparazzi, and fair use for taking photos in public. I pointed out the press box in the paper, the proficiency of the Post’s city editor Allyson Aleksey, and we discussed why a writer might want to use a pseudonym (pen name). Scherman asked about the state of print journalism versus digital. I suggested that online publications are still in a wild Students in Ted Scherman’s class learn about typewriters west-like stage, and looking for ways to charge for content. During COVID, despite news being consumed at a high level, the number of newspapers that went out of business increased by the hundreds. However, I shared my observation and belief that there is a nostalgia for printed newspapers. Now it was time for the students to be part of the story I would be writing, so I turned the camera over to a couple of Piedmont Post delivery kids in the class, Henry Call and Colby Hong, hoping they were as good at photography as they were at chucking a paper to front doors. articles.text: At the onset of the COVID- 19 pandemic, many pediatric services such as tutoring, counseling, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and other health care and educational services, switched from in-person to virtual formats. Initially, this transition was necessary due to quarantine conditions as we tried our best to support kids and families while unable to see them in-person. But now that practitioners have had a few years with this service delivery model, and are now presented with options: what does the future look like for pediatric services? Has teletherapy (via real time video conferencing) proven to be successful enough to sustain learning success and comparable to face-toface support? A review of the initial research reveals that teletherapy may be as effective as face-to-face interventions, across disciplines and for a variety of clinical outcomes. While there is more research to be done in this area, we are encouraged that the studies thus far do not demonstrate inferior outcomes with virtual vs in-person scenarios. The teletherapy studies examine 3 teletherapy models. First, teletherapy was shown to be successful in terms of providing educational information (written material, videos, etc.) directly to parents. Second, teletherapy was shown to be effective as a method of providing parent mediated support known as parent coaching in which, for example, the parent is Initial research indicates that teletherapy is effective. coached on how to implement a particular instructional or therapeutic program. And third, teletherapy was shown to be an effective platform for direct therapist/ child real-time treatment which shares many of the underlying principles as face-to-face therapy. There are obvious logistical advantages of teletherapy, such as reducing family stress during the busy after-school hours by cutting down on the amount of travel time needed to access the services and allowing children access to specialists who may be outside of the family’s geographic area. And there are obvious logistical elements, such as access to quality technology and physical home set up, which must be in place to ensure a successful virtual session. Taking into account these, and other logistical elements, can we develop a roadmap which allows service providers to maximally leverage the advantages provided by technology into our clinical practice ongoing, and provide families with increased access, options and convenience? Since the research is showing us that teletherapy is generally an effective service delivery model for educational and therapeutic services for children, perhaps over the next few years clinicians can focus on further exploration of questions such as for whom and under exactly which conditions is virtual vs in-person indicated. Katie Pengilly, MA, CCC, SLP, is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has announced that the annual Spring Fling gala, titled “Under a Piedmont Sky” this year, will be held in person on Friday, May 6 on Magnolia Avenue outside the Piedmont Center for the Arts and the new school theater. “We decided to have a blockparty style event this year,” said PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. “Piedmont has three years’ worth of elementary parents who haven’t experienced an in-person Spring Fling. We wanted to be able to share the fun with as many people as possible, as safely as possible.” Though the event hasn’t been held in town in many years, the foundation was determined to find a way to do it as part of building the elementary school community while showcasing Piedmont itself. The event will feature snacks, cocktails, a silent auction, and a set by Piedmont’s own Russell Simon, with popular bluegrass band Rusty Stringfield. “Spring Fling brings people together to share memories of the year that was, and to look forward to the year ahead, all over music, wine, and snacks,” said former Spring Fling Chair Amber Brumfiel. Andrea Horvath and Lisa Peters have been working closely with the City, police, fire, and school district to get the appropriate permits, keeping safety a priority. The January camp auction was successful, and there are a few parent theme parties being planned. An online auction will be available in April. Comings & Goings – portraits of students when they were in 1st grade and fifth grade – are on sale now at PiedmontSpringFling.org. This year’s fund-a-need will support PUSD’s Diversity, Equity and Inclusion programming. Funds raised through Spring Fling auctions and events directly support Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools. articles.text: Members of Highlander Robotics with their Engineering Inspiration Award. Twenty-five students from Highlander Robotics, Piedmont High School’s robotics team, traveled to UC Davis last weekend for the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Sacramento Regional Tournament and won an award that will take them to the FRC World Championship in Houston in three weeks. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game in January each year to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season, and competitions begin 8 weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game, called Rapid React, robots up to 120 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inch-wide tennis balls into an 8-foot high 4-foot wide funnel before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. Teams can win a number of awards based on the performance of their robots; the quality, innovation, and creativity of their designs; and the impact they make on their communities. In their first in-person regional tournament, the Highlanders competed with a 109- pound, 30-inch-square robot named “Selkie”. The tournament included 42 other teams who had come from as far as Mumbai and Taipei. After finishing 11 qualifying matches with a 7-win 4-loss record, the Highlanders ranked 5th, behind three former world champions and a veteran team from Orange County. After advancing to the playoffs as the third seeded alliance captain, the team won two straight quarterfinal matches before being eliminated in the semifinals by the second seed team captained by 2019 world champions, The Greybots, from Atascadero. In addition to bids to the world championship given to members of the winning alliance, two awards are given with the most prestigious judged awards, so some small hope remained. “It’s been a dream since 7th grade. I knew there was still a very slim chance but we’d been waiting through the awards and hadn’t gotten any”. When [they announced] we won the Engineering Inspiration Award, we were extremely surprised,” said team captain Charlie Lambert. The Engineering Inspiration award celebrates outstanding success in advancing respect and appreciation for engineering within a team’s community. This recognized their contributions in advocating for Piedmont High School’s new Fabrication Lab, supporting Piedmont Makers fundraiser for the lab, efforts towards gender parity on the team, and mentoring other local robotics teams. In addition to qualifying the team for the world championship, the team also had its $5000 registration fee sponsored by NASA. Selkie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Asha Byers and supported by drive coach Charlie Lambert, technician Valentina Prieto Black, and human player Arun Brahma. articles.text: Beat San Leandro 5-3, Castro Valley 3-1 Piedmont’s baseball team is coming off of two consecutive wins against upper Foothill Division opponents, defeating San Leandro 5-3 on Wednesday, March 23 at Humphries Diamond, and Castro Valley 3-1 at the Trojans’ field on Friday, March 25. The Highlanders won both games behind strong pitching performances of Tobin Cantrill and Alex Tafapolsky, who each recorded a complete game. Cantrill struck out seven San Leandro batters with two walks and hits allowed, while Tafapolsky also struck out seven in the game with Castro Valley, with four hits allowed and two walks. “They are throwing strikes and making the hitters feel uncomfortable, which is what we’re trying to do as a pitcher. Tobin has solidified himself as our number one guy. To carry a no-hitter into the sixth is a great feather in his cap,” said coach Eric Olson. Both seniors, it marked both pitchers’ first complete games. Cantrill carried a no-hitter heading into the top of the sixth inning. “I love playing with a lead and having that all the way to the sixth was great. articles.text: Photo by Mike McConathy Piedmont’s defense sets up against Encinal, a Shoreline Division team. As time continues to push toward the summer, more answers regarding the Piedmont High varsity football team are becoming firm. What we know is that the school will continues its historic 101-year varsity program. What we don’t is how the schedule will be created, or when, and with what teams. On March 15, Piedmont High principal Adam Littlefield announced at a virtual meeting with parents that four of the six teams in the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division voted to not revise their schedules to accommodate Piedmont. this means that PHS will not be eligible to schedule league opponents, win a league championship, or earn any All-League recipients. “San Lorenzo, Kennedy, Newark and Alameda said no. What I did was reach out to the principals we haven’t heard from, and my message for them was to have those principals nudge their athletic directors to connect with Bradley [Smet],” said Littlefield during the meeting. Smet also spoke at the virtual meeting and confirmed Piedmont would be ineligible for a league title in the WACC in 2022. “The downside in not being attached to the WACC is no league championship or league awards… Yes, it’s correct we’re not currently in the Shoreline. We could force a vote on the 17 total schools to let us in the Shoreline, but if everyone is saying ‘No’ in our league, is it the right thing to force a vote on the other schools,” asked Smet. Littlefield said that he has been working with WACC commissioner Dave Kiesel to find alternative options so Piedmont could have a standard 10-game schedule. He indicated that Kiesel is working with him to identify teams in the North Coast Section, Northern Section, Central Coast, and San Joaquin Sections that would be willing to play Piedmont. Littlefield added that PHS athletic director Bradley Smet is focusing on schools within the Central Coast (where he is from), Northern, and Sac-Joaquin sections and is hoping to schedule four home games and six away. This could mean a lot of driving for parents. PHS would be eligible to qualify for a postseason by finishing with a .500 overall record. Teams are typically eligible to qualify for the playoffs base on a number of factors. Without options in the Shoreline Division of WACC or North Coast Section, Piedmont must finish with a positive overall win-loss record. Littlefield confirmed that the high school will arrange and provide all transportation for away games. Piedmont’s non-league status also means that the Junior Varsity team must revise its schedule to fit with the varsity game plan. The school is now 12 days into the hunt for a new head football coach after officially posting job opening on Friday, March 18. What I did was reach out to the principals we haven’t heard from, and my message for them was to have those principals nudge their athletic directors to connect with Bradley [Smet],” said Littlefield during the meeting. Smet also spoke at the virtual meeting and confirmed Piedmont would be ineligible for a league title in the WACC in 2022. “The downside in not being attached to the WACC is no league championship or league awards… Yes, it’s correct we’re not currently in the Shoreline. We could force a vote on the 17 total schools to let us in the Shoreline, but if everyone is saying ‘No’ in our league, is it the right thing to force a vote on the other schools,” asked Smet. Littlefield said that he has been working with WACC commissioner Dave Kiesel to find alternative options so Piedmont could have a standard 10-game schedule. He indicated that Kiesel is working with him to identify teams in the North Coast Section, Northern Section, Central Coast, and San Joaquin Sections that would be willing to play Piedmont. Littlefield added that PHS athletic director Bradley Smet is focusing on schools within the Central Coast (where he is from), Northern, and Sac-Joaquin sections and is hoping to schedule four home games and six away. This could mean a lot of driving for parents. PHS would be eligible to qualify for a postseason by finishing with a .500 overall record. Teams are typically eligible to qualify for the playoffs base on a number of factors. Without options in the Shoreline Division of WACC or North Coast Section, Piedmont must finish with a positive overall win-loss record. Littlefield confirmed that the high school will arrange and provide all transportation for away games. Piedmont’s non-league status also means that the Junior Varsity team must revise its schedule to fit with the varsity game plan. articles.text: Staff Photos Wilson Wong had a productive game with seven aces against Hayward. The PHS boys’ volleyball team defeated Hayward, 3-0, on Thursday, March 24 at Binks Rawlings Gym, with game scores of 25-12, 25-12, 25-14. The team was still without setter Shunji Higashi, meaning the bulk of the roster had to step up. “Coming into this game, we knew that losing would put everything on a downhill slope. Hayward has had its program one year longer than us. It’s great to test how we are. We dominated and played strong,” said junior captain Wilson Wong. Piedmont did well in getting its serves in against Hayward, recording 12 aces on the night including seven from Wong, four from John Champion, and one by Kai Lambert. “I’ve been working really hard on consistency and my top-spin serves. John and I have really been working hard on our topserves, we want to build consistency,” said Wong. Piedmont’s front line was also productive with middle blockers Mason Kimball and Felix Broach, often getting their hands on spike attempts to block shots. “We really focused in practice on blocking. We figured it out; we’re a good defensive team,” said Kimball. The Highlanders opened the first set with a 5-0 lead thanks to four consecutive aces by Wong. The Highlanders then won another four consecutive points before a service error, 9-2, then five of the next six points for a 14-3 lead. Hayward inched back to 17-8, but Piedmont’s work in front of the net continued to limit attacking options. Broach had two blocks in the remaining points, and Kimball had a kill for set-point. In the second set, Piedmont started similarly with the first five points to jump ahead 5-1 PHS’ first seven points were thanks to errors from the Farmers when either defending or trying to create an attack with nearly all of their spike attempts sailing out of bounds. Kimball had two spikes to put PHS ahead 11-4, and had another three kills to help win the set, 25-12. Piedmont closed the third set with another 10-plus point victory, 25-14. This time, the Farms jumped out to a 6-3 advantage and increased it to 10-6. However, PHS scored the next five points to go ahead 11-10. The Farmers gained the next two points to re-gain the lead at 12-11, but the Highlanders scored the next 10 points with the help of a Kimball block and spike, and three aces by Champion – putting PHS up 21-12, with Wong finishing it off with two aces. articles.text: Diego Rivera’s massive mural “Pan American Unity” will be on display on the main floor at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art through summer 2023. On June 17, 2021, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco “Pan American Unity” was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to SFMOMA. The priceless 4,000-pound mural, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing about 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from its original location on Treasure Island. It is the largest of the artist’s works, and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the Diego Rivera Theater at City College. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, where it is now on display through 2023, when it will return to City College to be installed in a new performing arts center. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/ to learn more.
articles.title: Diego Rivera’s historic “Pan American Unity” mural on view at SFMOMA

articles.text: At the close of its 2022 season, San Francisco Ballet will honor the 37-year tenure of Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson with a gala performance. Tomasson has hand-selected ballets from the more than 50 works he choreographed and directed for San Francisco Ballet. articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir hosted its Making History Concert on Saturday, March 19 at First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The concert, which celebrated voices of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC), was filled with energizing performances from PEBCC’s four performing choirs and featured two world premieres, four student conductors, and one dance group reflecting the diverse East Bay community. A highlight of the night was Ecco’s Conducting Scholars, Tomo Takeuchi, George Mouratoff, Khoa Sands, and Anna Klein, conducting their peers in Estonian Lullabies. This was especially meaningful as Artistic Director, Eric Tuan, got his start conducting when he was a singer with the Choir. While each of the conductors had a different style, they demonstrated their ability to lead their peers through their interpretation of Veljo Tormis’ Estonian folk melodies with grace and expression. Ancora performed the World Premiere of A Portrait in Greys by local composer Jens Ibsen. Ibsen, who attended the concert, shared advice for young people about composing. “Own that you have something to say. I started as a singer and thought composing would be a hobby. I never could have dreamed I’d be doing things with my original music like I’m doing now…Composing means having something to say. You have to put that out there. Do yourself that kindness and go ahead and say it. The world is going to be better with more good music out there.” Ancora’s performance blended beautiful, haunting expressive vocal lines and crystal clear, well blended tone to bring this piece and the other selections to life. As the penultimate song of the evening, Ensemble performed a new piece, When I Sing, composed by Artistic Director Eric Tuan and commissioned by Yonchu Jenkins and Toshi Takeuchi. It was commissioned “to give back to the wonderful choir community and to show the beauty in music and the joy of singing as we emerge from these difficult times,” explained Tuan. Audience members couldn’t help but smile as the singers enveloped the concert hall in melodies of joy and optimism as they moved from singing to unison and ending the song in four-part harmony. The concert closed with Bolo Bolo Sab Mil Bolo, a collaboration between Ensemble and Kali Futnami’s youth bharatanatyam dancers. “The song is a well-loved devotional song to Shiva,” explained Futami. “Bharatanatyam dance is a very ancient South Indian classical dance form that is very rhythmic. The dancers helped to create the choreography. This is about Shiva, who is a dancer. The first sound of the universe is the sound of his drum, so the dancers show this and the little drum he carries. It was a full sensory experience as the dancers added movement and body percussion to Shiva Bhajan’s devotional song.” Bolo Bolo Ensemble and Kali Futnani dancers perform with Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir in a March 19 concert titled Making History. articles.text: Robert Redford and Nick Nolte star in A Walk in the Woods. A Walk in the Woods, released in 2015 and now streaming on Netflix and Prime, is a humorous geezer flick that is essentially a long hike on the Appalachian Trail, one in which two old friends renew an almost forgotten bond. Once the two central characters – Robert Redford as Bill Bryson and his out of shape bud, Stephen Katz, played by Nick Nolte – step off the parking lot tarmac and begin their journey, there’s not a lot to do other than put one foot in front of the other and engage in yearbook conversation. Nevertheless, this story has more than a few comic moments that made me smile and laugh out loud. Nolte as Katz is a hoot. When Bryson hit the trail, and later wrote the hugely popular novel of the same name, he was 47. Redford was heading toward 80, give or take, and Nolte was 74. These are not two guys having a midlife crisis, but perhaps hoping to encounter an epiphany in the backwoods while hiking the length of the Appalachian Trail, 2200 miles, from Georgia to Maine. In essence, they’re two codgers who’ve convinced themselves that a change of scenery (or a splash of adventure) might give than a fresh outlook on life. The film could have taken artistic license with the book and written lots of dialogue, even voice over, about how old guys just don’t casually sling a 60-pound pack over their aging shoulders and spend weeks walking through the Smokey Mountains, sleeping on the ground in their tent. When you’re 70+, the body has long ago begun to signal that “the golden years” was a slogan invented to sell cruise ship jaunts and never intended to indicate that you should be spending hours debating the efficacy of a hiking boot or a backpack with a kid in his early twenties who works at REI. A Walk in the Woods involves old dude conversations, but not how mortality haunts each day. Instead, they sit around a campfire and have friendly chats, and who better to do that than Nolte and Redford. There are more than a few gags, most taking place in small towns, off-trail. Katz has a conversation in a laundromat with a friendly, plus-size lady whose panties get caught in spin cycle and happens to have a jealous husband. Or the funny moment when they stop at a trail youth hostel, where Katz breaks the top bunk slats and lands on the bottom bunk on top of Bryson. One other thing: At the start of the hike, Katz and Bryson are almost like strangers. It’s been decades since they’ve hung out. But they work at what becomes an unforgettable reunion. Last point: Redford and Nolte are two actors who have demonstrated for decades that they can move across a wide spectrum of characters. Initially, Redford wanted to do this film with Paul Newman; instead, it remained on his shelf far too long. But as it turned out, that’s part of its charm. A Walk in the Woods. Directed by Ken Kwapis. Starring Robert Redford, Emma Thompson and Nick Nolte. 1 hr., 44 min. Rated R. Streaming on Netflix and Prime. Originally published in the Post in 2015.

articles.text: The Boy in the Striped Pajamas, released in 2008 and now streaming on Prime, is a heart-rending film, adapted from the young adult novel by John Boyle. This film is for middle school kids, teens and adults, and ideally should be watched with parents and discussed afterward. It captures the atrocities of the World War II Holocaust from the perspective of an 8-year-old boy, Bruno. The boy’s father is a high-ranking Nazi officer, Ralf (David Thewlis), who is promoted to be the commandant of what is euphemistically referred to as a “farm” somewhere in Poland. What this this means to Bruno is that he must leave Berlin, his familiar home and friends, and move to a remote countryside mansion where he feels suddenly isolated, lonely. Upon arriving, he is told by his mother, Elsa (Vera Farmiga), that he must not wander beyond the backyard wall or into the dense woods beyond. As an aside, it is evident that Elsa accepts the term “farm” without questioning her husband about his duties, initially basking in his prestigious position, and enjoying her large new home. Bruno and his older sister, Grete (Amber Beattie), instead of attending school are provided with a tutor, Herr Listz (Jim Norton), who fills his lessons with anti-Semitic propaganda. Grete covers the walls of her bedroom with posters of Hitler and Hitler youth. She is also enamored with a young, sadistic Nazi lieutenant, Kurt Kotler (Rupert Friend), his father’s adjutant. Bruno, soon feeling bored, begins to wander the compound, and though he has been admonished to remain within the walls, he finds a gate and ventures into the dense woods. He soon discovers a barbed-wire fence that encloses an expansive camp. On the other side of the wire he sees a boy his own age, wearing striped pajamas, and playing in the dirt. Sitting down on the other side of the fence, Bruno asks him his name. The boy stares through the fence, and finally says Shmuel (Jack Scanlon). Bruno, hungry for companionship, in all his innocence, begins what becomes an almost daily visit and conversation (he often brings the boy food), never suspecting that Shmuel is a prisoner and that the “farm” is, in reality, a death camp for Jews. Never revealing to his parents that he leaves the house grounds, or that he has found a new friend, Bruno, curious, does ask his mother about the smoke coming from the farm, and about the old man, Pavel (David Haymon), who works in their kitchen and is dressed in the same pants and shirt as is Shmuel. The answers to his questions are always vague. But unbeknownst to his father, Bruno does happen to watch him and a group of Nazi officers watching a propaganda film wherein the camp is shown to be a happy, almost joyous place for all those living inside the fence. One day Shmuel mentions that he can’t find his father, and Bruno offers to help find him. And so the boys devise a plan. Shmuel will bring a set of pajamas and cap (to hide Bruno’s unshaved head) the next day, and leaving his own clothes behind, Bruno crawls under the wire, dresses in the striped clothes, and the two will set off into the camp to locate the father. Watching the two walk together across a field, and toward the barracks in the distance, creates a chilling tableau. What awaits them is a truth beyond their comprehension. And it is a truth that Elsa has only recently come to suspect. And when she can’t find her son in the house or in the yard, she and Elsa begin a search w that is terrifying (she later calls Ralf), as is the conclusion of this powerful film. The Boy in the Striped Pajamas. Directed by Mark Herman. Released in 2008 by Miramax Films. Starring Asa Butterfield, Vera Farmiga, and David Thewlis. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on Prime.

articles.text: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen (aka T-2), released in 2009 like its precursor is a kid magnet. This big tent franchise is loud, kinetic and superbly stylized. It is based on Hasboro toys, those plastic robots (Autobots and Decepticons) that can be transformed into machinery and were featured in television cartoons and comic books. The first film, T-1, directed by Michael Bay, grossed $708 million worldwide, won three awards for visual effects and was nominated for three Academy Awards. The story was original (if a bit convoluted) and a veritable buffet of CGI and surround sound. At the center of the original Transformers is Sam Witwicky (Shia LaBeouf) and Mikaela Barnes (Megan Fox), high school seniors, who find themselves caught up in an ancient struggle between the evil Decepticons (Megatron, Blackout, Scorponok, Frenzy, Barricade, Devastator) and the good Autobots (Optimus Prime, Jazz, Bumblebee, Ironhide, Ratchet). Though it’s more a ride than a story – more action than introspection – embedded in the movie is a coming of age, first car, first girlfriend narrative that is sweet and compelling. The challenge for the T-2 sequel was how to recapture those jaw-dropping moments when, for the first time, filmgoers watched in stunned silence as incredible pieces of machinery were transformed into Bots, good and bad, followed by sounds of metal tearing, and orange volcaA scene from Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen. nic explosions. Regrettably, T-2 is unable to fulfill the visceral excitement of T-1. The magic of the Bots transforming is now familiar. The Bot battle scenes, still a ballet of destruction, seem almost predictable. The chemistry between Sam and Mikaela is well established and reduced to whether they will actually say to one another, “I love you.” Is it a cinematic spectacle, a ride to be enjoyed for the sheer, overwhelming special effects and visual artistry? Indeed. But the story – the resurrection of the Decepticons (Megatron, buried in the Laurentian Abyss, in particular) and their search for the All Spark – has grown even thinner. The screenwriters, likely sensing their own lack of inspiration, attempt to jack up the script with comic relief. John Turturro’s role as Agent Simmons in T-1 is reprised only to descend into silliness. Most egregious is the stereotyping of two new Autobots, Skids and Mudflap, two trashtalking Bot-homies from the hood. The only thing they’re not wearing is black face. Though meant to be funny, they are simply evidence of the obvious cultural and racial myopia of the writers and the director and a failure to find something to write about that is fresh and gripping. Putting all that aside, T-2 earned its keep at the box office. There are fans of the franchise as loyal as those Potter heads who, like the Transformer crowd, believe not in the destination but in the journey. Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen. Starring Shia LaBeouf, Megan Fox, Josh Duhamel. Directed by Michael Bay. 2 hrs., 29 min. Rated PG-13. Reprinted from 2009.

articles.text: Archaeologists continue to make some of the most marvelous discoveries. While we look into the deepest recesses of humanity, we find that we are able to look at ourselves in the mirror. Pictorial art dates back to Neanderthal days; approximately 64,000 years ago. Homo sapiens left cave paintings in Chauvet and Lascaux. Less is known about prehistoric musical instruments. Logic tells us that music must have played an important part from the beginning. Children do not need to be taught to clap their hands. Early humans surely must have learned to sing simply by discovering their own voices or listening to the howl of animals. There is an Italian saying: “anyone who has a voice can sing”. Instrumental music developed later. The earliest musical instrument discovered was a Neanderthal flute made of bone some 50,000 to 60,000 years ago. Early humans made flutes of bone and wood. Early trumpets were made from the horns of animals. The earliest stringed instruments developed at the same time as the bow and arrow. With civilization came the development of music notation. The Sumerians used music notation and the Greeks were past masters of the musical art. These were the inspirations for modern opera. Somewhat akin to opera is the Requiem. For sheer drama, nothing tops the Requiem by Verdi. The Stabat Mater by Dvorak probes the human soul. This past weekend I discovered another great work, this one a German Requiem by Johannes Brahms. In two performances under the inspired direction of David Morales, both concerts featured Morales’ Cantare Chorale, a full symphony orchestra, spoken reflection by six young poets, and professional vocal soloists soprano Shawnette Sulker and baritone Torlef Borsting. If memory serves me correctly, Morales has been an inspiration in the East Bay community for some 50 years. He exemplifies the best of the unification of humanity. The chorus and orchestra are all ages, ethnicities and abilities. They all come together to express the highest ideals of humanity. And now a word about the PCO The same can be said of our own Piedmont Chamber Orchestra. Let us hope that the difficulties of the COVID pandemic are waning. The 4 p.m. concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday afternoon, March 26, was a festive event. A large audience was enthusiastic in its response. And the orchestra responded and played its heart out. It also helped to have Martha Stoddard as the conductor and Stuart Gronningen as manager. The Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is a community effort – the city’s hometown orchestra. It includes professional musicians playing alongside amateurs both old and young. articles.text: Local pottery makers and ceramicists will discuss their artistry this Sunday, April 3, in an event hosted by Oakland Museum of California. Oakland Museum of California will host an informational discussion with Bay Area potters and ceramicists this Sunday, April 3, in the James Moore Theater. Featured local artists include Rosa Dorantes, Viviana Matsuda, and Chinzalee Sonami. The discussion will be held in conjunction with the museum’s ongoing exhibition, Edith Heath: A Life in Clay. The event will be moderated by Dorantes, Head of Ceramics at the Crucible, in a discussion with Sonami of Pala Ceramics in Oakland, and Mutsuda of Mud Witch in San Francisco. The event, titled “What Does it Mean to Endure?”, reflects on artistry and entrepreneurship. The three female artists will discuss Heath’s legacy in pottery and ceramics, and her uses of materials that are sustainable and easily found in California. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her designs and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than traditional white clay for dinnerware. The James Moore Theatre is located in the museum at 1000 Oak Street. Masks will continue to be required for all visitors, regardless of vaccination status. Adults must show proof of vaccination along with photo identification. Capacity is limited. The event will be held from 2 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. Visit ht t ps://museumca. org/2022/what-does-it-mean-endure-conversation-bay-area-potters to obtain tickets.

articles.text: Nº 51 in a biweekly series I first met Terrance Gelenter when Guy and Jeanine Saperstein invited Michael and me to a club date at the Hotel Madison to hear him sing music from the American Songbook. They had heard him perform before Christmas holidays, and Terrance was back on the microphone last weekend, and was even better. He had proved to the Hotel Madison that he could fill the place and keep the wait-staff busy serving drinks. The club had a great vibe and the tunes flowed, ballads of the 1940s to 1960s, along with the 1939 jewel, Somewhere Over the Rainbow. Accompanied by Sheldon Forrest on keyboard, Terrance started with Chances Are, originally recorded by San Francisco native Johnny Mathis, As I closed my eyes, I was back in Teen Town, dancing cheek to cheek. As Sheldon played the first few notes, anticipation hung in the air, then the audience sighed in recognition. Terrance’s resonant voice filled the space, transforming a hotel breakfast room into a New York City jazz club. He deftly channels the greats of musical song, taking us a world away from Brooklyn, where in a prior life, he was a schmatta salesman in the New York garment trade. His story is not so different from many of us expats who left the good life for the shores of faraway places. At age 60, he recast himself to become a Parisian and brought along his musical gifts of song, openheartedly sharing the gem-like lyrics with emotional clarity as crisp as salty chips. Terrance likes to include the preludes to songs from a time when lyricists wrote more good verse than put to music. He morphed into Tony Bennett and Because of You, where he playfully parroted Bennett’s Queens accent for a moment. Then, Fly Me to the Moon, at ringside with Sinatra. Then, Johnny Mathis, When Sunny Gets American vocalist Terrance Gelenter at Café Les Deux Magots at 6 Place Saint-Germain des Prés, a favorite of his. Blue, and Side-2 of Wonderful, Wonderful. He sang Smile in Nat King Cole’s original arrangement and reminded us that Charlie Chaplin is given credit as composer (it was in his 1936 movie Modern Times). Playing the cards we’re dealt The gig economy is not what is normally associated with retired people. In the U.S., the hard boundary between “work” and “retirement” and even the touchstone of retirement age of 65 has blurred as people write a second act to their work life. Employer-paid pensions, except government jobs, fell out along the way, and older adults feel pressured to keep working. articles.text: Many expenses in life are unpredictable. But there are two things you know you’ll have to pay for: medical bills and retirement. You’ll probably need to take a variety of steps to meet these costs, but one financial instrument that can help is a health savings account (HSA). If you’re not familiar with an HSA, here are the basics: • Eligibility – If you are enrolled in a qualified high-deductible health plan (HDHP), you can generally contribute to an HSA. While HSAs are typically offered through employers, you can still open one if your employer doesn’t provide it, or if you’re self-employed, although you must have HDHP coverage. You also can’t be enrolled in another health insurance plan, other than those permitted, such as dental, vision, long-term care and disability insurance, and you can’t be enrolled in Medicare. Also, you can’t be claimed as a dependent on another person’s tax return. • Contribution limits – In 2022, you can put in up to $3,650 to an HSA if you have single coverage, or $7,300 for family coverage. And if you’re 55 or older, you can put in an extra $1,000 per year. • Tax benefits – An HSA has triple tax advantages: Your contributions are made with pre-tax dollars, so they can reduce your taxable income for the year; your earnings grow taxfree; and your withdrawals are tax-free, provided the money is used for qualified medical expenses. (Withdrawals taken before age 65 that aren’t used for qualified medical expenses are taxable and subject to a 20% penalty; once you reach 65, the penalty no longer applies, although withdrawals are still taxable.) In addition to its providing tax benefits, an HSA can help you in other ways. Perhaps most significantly, your HSA can be an additional financial resource for your retirement. That’s because the money in your HSA can be carried over from year to year – you aren’t obligated to “use it or lose it.” So, the money not spent on annual medical expenses can continue to grow tax-deferred. Plus, an HSA is “portable” – it moves with you when you leave a job. Furthermore, unlike a 401(k) or a traditional IRA, an HSA does not require you to begin taking withdrawals once you reach 72 – you can leave your account untouched for essentially as long as you’d like. And while you may need to use your HSA funds to meet your medical expenses in retirement – which can be considerable, even with Medicare – you can use what you don’t spend on medical costs for your other needs without penalty, once you reach age 65. (As mentioned above, any HSA withdrawals not used for qualified medical costs are taxable.) Here’s one other point to keep in mind: Your HSA likely contains investment options, along with a cash account. If you put all your funds in the cash account, as many people do, you might be depriving yourself of the growth opportunities provided by the investment options. On the other hand, of course, these investments generally carry more risk. One possible way to benefit from both parts of your HSA is to keep enough cash to cover your health insurance’s out-of-pocket maximum and invest the rest. As you can see, an HSA can help you in numerous ways. If you have access to one, consider taking advantage of it. Last Wednesday, March 23, was the first Wednesday of spring, and another beautiful day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group’s weekly walk. There was a solid turnout of 30 walkers and one K-9 best friend. Noemi Alvarado announced that the group’s official Piedmont Heritage Tree submission had been sent to the city. It is the large redwood at the entrance to Wildwood Gardens. Winners will be announced at the City Arbor Day festivities on April 28. Spring brings with it beautiful flowers which adds to the enjoyment of walking Piedmont’s streets. The group headed off, going up Highland Avenue past the trees with wonderful, white blossoms in upper Piedmont Park, and then went down to the crosswalk at Sheridan Avenue. They crossed the street and saw the house on the corner had gotten a head start on another type of hunt. On its front yard lawn were about a dozen very large, different colored, plastic Easter eggs. At the corner of with Lakeview and Sheridan the houses on both sides of the street have large dogwoods with delicate, white flower petals. Going up Lakeview, they saw the very tall, old redwoods that shade the street. The story was told that over a hundred years ago the man who built the beautiful home, a little further up the hill at the corner of Sea View and Lincoln Avenues, was a lumber baron who loved redwoods and he planted them around his estate. On their way up Lakeview, the group saw an opening between a set of redwoods in a front yard. During the windstorm in January, one of the redwoods came crashing down, taking out trees on its way, and falling into the street. At the top of Lakeview the group went on Sea View. At its corner with Lincoln Avenue, they saw the home built by a lumber baron and owned for many years by Senator William Knowland, the U.S. Senate majority leader during the Eisenhower Administration in the 1950s and owner and publisher of the Oakland Tribune. The group went down Lincoln one block to King Avenue and down King to Crocker Park, were the walkers enjoyed seeing the azaleas, fruit tree blossoms, dogwoods, calla lilies, and other flowers. The walkers emerged on Hampton Road and went onto Sea View where they were treated to the sight of a veritable forest of different colored tulips in the front yard of the Reich family. The walkers made their way back to King with a one-block walk up Farragut Avenue, and then continued down King to La Salle Avenue. Along the way, there was a wonderful, exotic front yard garden to see. On a past walk the group had met the homeowner who told them the story of the garden’s creation. It was originally a typical Piedmont front yard, but he had an inspiration. A neighbor was doing an excavation and had a truckload of dirt that he was willing to trade for a case of beer. The mound of dirt provided the base for this large garden of tropical plants. Jim Kellogg and Mike Henn were on the Piedmont Planning Commission at the time and told the group about the challenging approval process for the unusual landscape design, which turned out to be wonderful. Crossing Crocker Avenue they came to a yard with two gorgeous dogwoods and more beautiful spring flowers. Further on, red buds and striking red leaf maples added even more color to this spring walk. The walkers turned down Woodland Way where it meets La Salle. They noted that repair work was being done on the roof of a home that had been damaged when a large tree fell on it during the January windstorm. Further up Woodland the walkers were charmed by wisterias on the two sides of a garage and the purple f loral frame around its entrance that the plants made. Even though the group was a little behind schedule for a noontime return to the center of town, they couldn’t resist taking a side trip onto secluded Wistaria Way loop. They returned by way of Wildwood Gardens, where passed the group’s redwood Heritage Tree submission. It had been over a three-mile tour of Piedmont’s beautiful spring trees, plants, and flowers; and felt like a walk in a big, wonderful park during the first week of spring. articles.text: To keep your body running at peak performance, it needs regular maintenance: a spring tune-up, so to speak. The lovely spring days we are experiencing now encourage us to exercise by getting out and walking or taking an aerobics class. In our haste to firm up our body by heading to the gym, let’s not forget the need to exercise our brain as well. Did you know there are few things that stimulate the brain the way music does? Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine have found that listening to music can reduce anxiety, blood pressure, and pain. Plus, they found that music can help improve sleep quality, mood, mental alertness, and memory. If you want to keep your brain engaged throughout the aging process, it seems like listening to or playing music is a great tool. It can provide a total brain workout. So just how does music do this? Music can activate almost all brain regions and networks. Thus, music can help us keep our brain pathways strong, including networks that are involved in well-being, cognitive function, quality of life, and happiness. In fact, studies show there is only one other situation in which you can activate so many brain networks at once, and that is when you participate in social activities. Here at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, we firmly believe in the benefits of music. As a social activity we have an active Glee Club because the act of singing lowers stress and releases endorphins that help make us happy. Research also shows that choir singing releases an antibody which boosts our Members of The Lake Merritt Glee Club, Laura McGee (left), Pat King, and Diane Livingston singing “Give My Regards to Broadway.” immune system. Further, singing has been shown to enhance the memory part of the brain. With the pandemic waning, The Lake Merritt is happy to welcome back live music into our community on a weekly basis. The Jazz Therapists, featuring local jazz performer Anna de Leon, performed in The Terrace Room just last week. This seven-member band plays in communities for older adults throughout the Bay Area. Our residents enjoy the music and many also take to the dance floor in the Terrace Room, which overlooks Lake Merritt. If you are interested in some everyday brain boosts from music, you may want to try these ideas. Try listening to what your kids or grandkids are listening to. New music challenges the brain in a way that old music does not. It might not feel pleasurable at first, but that unfamiliarity forces the brain to struggle to understand the new sound. You can also change the color of your cursor, by going to System Preferences/Accessibility/ Display/Pointer/Pointer Color. This feature can be useful if you have a dark Desktop Picture on your Mac. 4. You can now save pictures to your Photos library directly from the Messages app on your computer. articles.text: On a beautiful day in March, the Piedmont Seniors visited the historic McConaghy House in Hayward on a monthly outing. When Scottish-Irish immigrant Neal McConaghy built his home in 1888, his youngest son, John, lived there until he passed away at age 100. After John’s death, there were plans to demolish this historic home for retail space. Fortunately, concerned citizens halted ideas for demolition in 1972, and the property was purchased by the Hayward Area Recreation District (HARD). It reopened as a museum, curated and managed by employees and volunteers in 1976. This stately Victorian has authentic period pieces of furniture, floor and wall coverings. Due to its age, the McConaghy House is not ADA compliant, but the house was so interesting the Seniors found the nine exterior stairs easily worth it. There are two parlors, one for family and one for visitors. This is an interesting concept as the house was considered “middle-class” in its day. Located at 18701 Hesperian Boulevard in Hayward, it is open on some Saturdays or by appointment. Donations are welcome to help maintain the integrity of the home. After the house tour, the Piedmont Seniors collectively satisfied their appetites with lunch at a wonderful Italian restaurant, Buon Appetito. The restaurant could rival any of the best dining spots in San Francisco, and with much more reasonable pricing. All agreed that the tiramisu was the most delicious we have ever tasted and is made on site daily. The outdoor dining made for a very pleasant dining experience. To finish off the day, the Seniors went to a little-known oasis in Hayward, the Japanese Gardens, the oldest Japanese garden in California. It is also managed by the Hayward Recreation The Piedmont Seniors recently visited the historic McConaghy House in Hayward. District. This garden is situated next to Hayward’s Senior Center and adjacent to the Douglas Morrisson Theatre. The garden follows the Japanese principles of design, while using California native stone and plants. This 3.5 acres of serenity is the perfect place for weddings, or simply to meditate in a beautiful environment. It is also free for visitors. Though many of the Piedmont Seniors have lived in the East Bay for years, no one from the group had ever previously discovered this hidden gem. The Japanese Gardens are one of Hayward’s many jewels. They are a tribute to Hayward’s long history and kinship with the Japanese people and culture. A must-see for visitors and locals alike, the gardens are open from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily.

articles.text: The remarkable Robert (“Bob”) Kingsbury Lane, a loving husband, father, grandfather, brother, and friend, passed away on February 19, 2022, at the age of 77. Robert spent his last day surrounded by family and the beauty of nature on a sunny and secluded Santa Cruz beach, soaking his feet in the Pacific Ocean and delighting his grandkids with treasures he’d sifted from the sand. Robert was born September 1, 1944, the first son of Jack and Trudy Lane of Los Angeles and older brother to Christopher. A 3rd generation Californian, he was raised in Pacific Palisades and received his high school diploma from Harvard School. A life-long learner, Robert attended the University of California in Berkeley where he pursued many academic passions, including architecture and photography. While there, he made many of his enduring friendships as a member of the Psi Upsilon fraternity. After graduating with a Bachelor’s degree in history, Robert returned to Los Angeles to earn his Juris Doctor at Loyola Law School. Prior to beginning his legal career, Robert heeded the call and served in the United States Army as a First Lieutenant, stationed in Baltimore, Maryland. Though he served during a time of social and political turbulence, Robert remained guided by his personal ethos and completed his service honorably as a conscientious objector. It was in Baltimore where Robert met his wife, Reiko. While on day-leave from military assignment, Robert wandered into the historic Peabody Institute in the city’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, drawn by the 19th century architecture. There, Robert discovered Reiko playing the pipe organ in an out-of-the-way practice room. Returning weekly to listen to her play, Robert and Reiko eventually married in California and moved to Piedmont to live, work, and raise their family. They were married for 50 years and had three daughters. Fiercely principled, staunchly free-thinking, and endlessly engaged, Robert was a vigorous advocate for his clients, friends and loved ones, and as a global citRobert Lane izen. Over the many decades that Robert practiced law under his own banner, R. Kingsbury Lane, Inc., he never had to market his services. Referrals and long-held contacts made up his loyal client list. As “Dad” to his daughters Nysa, Mari, and Lindsay, he was a coach, tutor, musical troupe manager, camp leader, Fourth of July fireworks scofflaw, “party favor” distributor, constant champion, and life-long trusted advisor on things great and small. Perhaps above all, Robert instilled in his daughters the importance of independent thinking, self-reliance, and fighting for what you believe in. He modeled these values himself as a vocal and action-oriented proponent of social and environmental justice. Robert viewed the world through the lens of an artist. His poetry captured the emotion and essence of its subject; his camera seized the candid, the wild, the unexpected, the golden hour moments; his sketches were never constrained by what was, only what could be. In the family’s overwhelming grief at losing him, we try to see his life as he would - beautifully, and uncommonly well-lived. Robert is survived by his wife Reiko, daughters Nysa, Mari, and Lindsay, five beloved grandchildren, his brother Christopher Lane, cousins John Hogle and Barbara Clement, and many nieces and nephews. A celebration of life will be held on Sunday, May 1st at 2 p.m. at the First Unitarian Universalist Church of San Francisco.
